The Speedup Paradox: Rethinking Inference Speed-Quality Trade-off in Embodied Tasks

Yujin Wang   Junli Chen   Yixuan Li   Shunan Dong Affiliation: Huazhong Yang   Yongpan Liu   Hongyang Jia Affiliation: Tsinghua University Email: yujin-wa24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    hjia@tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Embodied foundation models have recently been widely used to improve robot generalization and task success rates. Previous works apply lossy efficient-inference techniques such as quantization, pruning, and asynchronous inference, accepting small action quality degradation in exchange for lower per-step computation cost and inter-action latency. However, unlike traditional static ML tasks, embodied tasks involve repeated interaction with the environment, and task-level performance is determined not only by per-step cost, but also by closed-loop effects unique to embodied execution, which remain insufficiently characterized in current efficient-inference studies. In this work, we propose TISED (Task-level Inference Speedup Effect Decomposition), an analytical framework that unifies diverse lossy inference optimization techniques and decomposes their effects on static and dynamic tasks, and uncovers some paradoxical effects on task-level performance: (1) on static tasks, optimization sometimes can lengthen end-to-end per-task completion time even as per-step latency drops; (2) on dynamic tasks, moderate lossy optimization can raise task success rate even above the baseline; and (3) the monotonicity and sweet-spot location of both effects can shift with hardware configuration. Together, our findings provide a new perspective on adapting inference optimization techniques to embodied tasks.

Keywords: Embodied Tasks, Lightweight, Quantization, Pruning, Hardware-Software Co-design, Asynchronous Inference.

1 Introduction

Embodied models such as Vision-Language-Action models (VLA) [24, 44, 6, 5, 8, 7, 40, 33] and World-Action Models (WAM) [23, 25, 57, 56] have been widely deployed across diverse embodied scenarios. These models are typically obtained by fine-tuning large-scale pretrained vision-language models [58, 4] and world models [2, 16], yielding strong cross-task generalization and improved robustness to environmental variation. However, to fully accommodate these capabilities, they usually have large parameter counts and compute FLOPs at inference time, posing a key barrier to edge deployment and real-time control.

To address this, many recent works apply lossy inference optimization techniques to embodied models, such as quantization [59, 54], cache reuse [53, 28, 48], sampling step reduction [34, 11, 50], and asynchronous scheduling [46, 43, 35]. These methods have been shown to reduce per-step inference latency or shorten the gap between consecutive action chunks with slight accuracy degradation. Embodied tasks, however, differ fundamentally: Each cycle of the inference-execution loop consists of one policy inference and the subsequent action execution, and the loop runs for many such cycles before a rollout terminates. The per-step latency reductions from these methods therefore capture only a fragment of task-level performance: they ignore how many cycles the rollout ultimately requires until success, how the environment evolves during model inference, and how all of these interact with hardware performance across inference and execution costs.

To analyze how lossy inference optimization shapes embodied task performance beyond per-step latency, we propose TISED (Task-level Inference Speedup Effect Decomposition) analysis in Figure 1. First, we place policy-intrinsic and execution-aware optimization on a common per-chunk time formula. Building on this unified view, we model the end-to-end objective separately for the two task regimes: on static tasks, end-to-end completion time is jointly determined by the per-chunk inference time and the number of chunks that the full rollout requires; on dynamic tasks, task success rate is jointly determined by action quality and observation staleness.

We empirically test these predictions with a progressive-lightweighting sweep across task types, model backbones, optimization methods, and compute platforms, from which three observations emerge: (1) On static tasks, end-to-end completion time is sometimes non-monotonic in the lightweighting strength due to the deterioration of action quality (per-step inference latency reduction ≠\neq end-to-end per-task latency reduction). (2) On dynamic tasks, task success rate is sometimes non-monotonic in the lossy optimization strength due to the trade-off between degraded action quality and reduced observation staleness (static task accuracy ≠\neq dynamic task accuracy). (3) Fixing the task and lightweighting method, the above trends and the location of the sweet spot shifts with the hardware compute budget. Together, these three observations show that the per-step speed-quality trade-off familiar from static ML no longer predicts task-level outcomes in embodied closed-loop execution—speed and quality interact through rollout length, action delay, and hardware budget.

2 Related Works

2.1 Embodied Foundation Models

Recent progress in vision-language-action models (VLA) [24, 44, 6, 5, 8, 7, 40, 33] and world-action models (WAM) [23, 25, 57, 56] have enabled stronger open-world generalization, task adaptation, and large-scale policy transfer. However, these capabilities come at a high inference cost. For example, by default π0\pi_{0} [6] (3.3B parameters) is deployed on high-end consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090, and Cosmos-Policy [23] (2B parameters) on datacenter-class accelerators such as H100. This is a key barrier to edge deployment and low-latency control. In this work, rather than scaling capabilities or enhancing generalization, we study how to deploy these models efficiently in the inference-execution loop.

2.2 Lossy Optimizations for Embodied Model Inference

To reduce the computational burden of embodied models, recent work has explored a range of lossy lightweight inference strategies. These methods can be grouped into two categories: (1) Policy-intrinsic optimization, which reduces the cost of each forward pass through techniques such as quantization [59, 54, 49, 55], denoise step reduction [20, 41, 13, 27], and cache reuse [53, 28, 48, 61]. For example, Q-VLA [54] analyzes how different components of a VLA vary in quantization sensitivity and assigns mixed precision accordingly to minimize the resulting action error; VLA-Cache [53] exploits the sparsity of background visual information across perception steps and reuses less-salient tokens to reduce redundant computation. (2) Execution-aware optimization, which improves effective control frequency by overlapping inference with execution, such as asynchronous scheduling [46, 43, 35]. For example, VLASH [46] rolls the robot state forward using the previously generated action chunk to predict the state at execution time, and further reduces prediction-execution misalignment by fine-tuning. Most of these works focus only on reducing the latency of a single inference, leaving a systematic analysis of end-to-end effects in embodied scenarios largely unexplored. In this work, rather than targeting a specific lightweight algorithm, we provide a unified modeling framework to analyze the unique impact of such algorithms on embodied tasks.

2.3 Efficiency-Accuracy Trade-off Characterizations

Aggressive lossy optimization methods can achieve significant gains in latency or energy efficiency while harming the accuracy. Previous works such as Deep Compression [17] established a trade-off between efficiency and accuracy in deep learning models. Subsequently, a lot of research has attempted to push this Pareto frontier forward in vision and language models [18, 51, 31, 30, 62]. In embodied systems, this relationship becomes more complex due to error accumulation and closed-loop feedback. Works such as [26, 22] introduced a new trade-off between efficiency and accuracy in time-sensitive tasks, but their scope was limited to object detection or LLM agents. Works such as [61, 21, 45] have characterized the inference performance of VLA models across various hardware devices but lack task-level performance. Work [29] provides valuable analysis of the negative impact of model lightweighting on execution in embodied task scenarios, while their focus is on the negative side. In this work, we further explore the synergy between the positive and negative effects of lightweight optimization and conduct a cross-hardware study.

3 Task-Level Inference Speedup Effect Decomposition

Embodied inference optimization operates within an inference-execution loop, not during a single forward pass. Therefore, a per-step speedup does not translate directly into a task-level gain: it changes both how many control cycles a rollout needs and how stale the observation is when the resulting action is executed. These two effects give rise to different failure modes in different task regimes. We develop this view into TISED, which analyzes task-level performance across lightweighting strength, task dynamics, and hardware budget. TISED places policy-intrinsic and execution-aware optimization on a common closed-loop time axis, and separates the end-to-end effect into cycle time, rollout length, and action delay.

We use two task regimes throughout the paper. In a static task, the task-relevant environment state remains effectively unchanged during model inference (e.g., static pick & place task). In this regime, lightweighting primarily affects movement smoothness and total execution time. In a dynamic task, the task-relevant environment state evolves while the model is still computing the next action (e.g., picking a rolling ball or playing ping-pong). In this regime, lightweighting changes both action quality and reaction speed – the inference speed directly affects the policy’s ability to react to dynamic environments. More detailed analysis and derivation can be found in Appendix A.

3.1 Closed-Loop Timing Model

As shown in Figure , let TinfT_{\mathrm{inf}} be the latency of one full-model policy inference, nn the action chunk size [60], and TactT_{\mathrm{act}} the duration of one action. In the synchronous full-model baseline, one chunk consists of one inference followed by nn executed actions. We use this baseline chunk time as the reference cost:

Policy-intrinsic methods reduce computation inside the policy network. We represent their timing effect by a latency ratio α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1]. This ratio can be changed by adjusting the number of quantization layers, the pruning ratio, and so on. Under this class of methods, the realized per-chunk time and per-chunk speedup are:

Execution-Aware Optimization.

Execution-aware methods like asynchronous inference change how inference is scheduled with robot execution, and they usually require complex system scheduling. To simplify the analysis, we performed abstract modeling of asynchronous inference by emulating work [46]. We summarize the scheduling knob by an action overlap depth n′∈{0,…,n}n^{\prime}\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, the number of primitive actions whose execution can overlap with the next inference. The realized per-chunk time and per-chunk speedup are:

Tcycleea​(n′)=Tinf+n​Tact−min⁡{Tinf,n′​Tact},ηchunkea​(n′)=TchunkTcycleea​(n′).\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{cycle}}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=T_{\mathrm{inf}}+nT_{\mathrm{act}}-\min\{T_{\mathrm{inf}},n^{\prime}T_{\mathrm{act}}\},\quad\eta_{\mathrm{chunk}}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=\frac{T_{\mathrm{chunk}}}{T_{\mathrm{cycle}}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})}.

By overlapping the next inference with the current chunk’s execution, each new action is computed from an observation taken before those actions complete, so the policy acts on an increasingly outdated view of the environment and also degrades the action quality.

End-to-End Time.

A complete embodied task spans many action chunks. The total number of chunks is not a fixed constant: it is an outcome of the rollout under the selected optimization. For the baseline and the two optimization classes, the task completion times are:

Per-task time therefore need not track per-step time, and may even move in the opposite direction.

Action Delay.

We also track the residual action delay, i.e., the time from an observation to the first action that can be executed from the corresponding policy output:

Dactbase\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{base}} =Tinf,Dactpl(α)=αTinf,Dactea(n′)=max{0,Tinf−n′Tact}.\displaystyle=T_{\mathrm{inf}},\quad D_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)=\alpha T_{\mathrm{inf}},\quad D_{\mathrm{act}}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=\max\{0,T_{\mathrm{inf}}-n^{\prime}T_{\mathrm{act}}\}. (6)

Dynamic-task analysis further depends on DactD_{\mathrm{act}}, which captures the observation staleness accumulated by the time the corresponding action executes. To cover both policy-intrinsic and execution-aware optimization, let uu denote the operating point of the chosen method: u=αu=\alpha for policy-intrinsic optimization and u=n′u=n^{\prime} for execution-aware optimization. We use a structured surrogate to capture the two dominant factors in dynamic success:

P^succ​(u)\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{succ}}(u) =Φ(q(u),z(u)),z(u)=Dact(u)ωenv,∂Φ/∂q≥0,∂Φ/∂z≤0.\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(q(u),z(u)\right),\qquad z(u)=D_{\mathrm{act}}(u)\omega_{\mathrm{env}},\qquad\partial\Phi/\partial q\geq 0,\qquad\partial\Phi/\partial z\leq 0. (7)

where q⁡(u)q(u) represents the action quality, ωenv\omega_{\mathrm{env}} is the environment change rate (e.g., conveyor speed or moving-target velocity), z⁡(u)=Dact​(u)​ωenvz(u)=D_{\mathrm{act}}(u)\omega_{\mathrm{env}} measures how far the environment drifts during the action delay, and Φ\Phi maps these two factors to a success rate. In words: dynamic success goes up when actions are more accurate, and goes down when the environment has drifted far from what the policy actually saw. As lightweighting strengthens, q⁡(u)q(u) typically falls (less computation or staler input) while z⁡(u)z(u) may also fall (faster inference shortens the observation-to-action gap). The outcome for dynamic-task success therefore depends on the relative strength of these two trends.

Compute Hardware.

The timing terms above are not intrinsic to the policy alone. TinfT_{\mathrm{inf}} is determined by the compute platform that runs the policy, whereas TactT_{\mathrm{act}} is fixed by the robot execution side and the task setting. (1) For static tasks, let ρ=Tinf/Tact\rho=T_{\mathrm{inf}}/T_{\mathrm{act}} denote the inference-to-execution time ratio. For a fixed task and a fixed optimization setting, the per-chunk speedups can be written as:

ηchunkpl​(ρ)\displaystyle\eta_{\mathrm{chunk}}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\rho) =ρ+nα​ρ+n,ηchunkea(ρ)=ρ+nρ+n−min⁡{ρ,n′}.\displaystyle=\frac{\rho+n}{\alpha\rho+n},\quad\eta_{\mathrm{chunk}}^{\mathrm{ea}}(\rho)=\frac{\rho+n}{\rho+n-\min\{\rho,n^{\prime}\}}. (8)

It means that the same lightweighting setting can yield different task-level effects on different compute platforms. (2) For dynamic tasks, the delay DactD_{\rm act} can also be impacted by hardware ability, thereby affecting z⁡(u)z(u) and P^succ​(u)\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{succ}}(u).

4 Experiments

Section 3 shows that per-step latency is an incomplete proxy for embodied inference optimization. In this section, we empirically characterize how this proxy breaks down through controlled sweeps of lightweighting across task regimes, policy models, optimization methods, and compute platforms. These sweeps are designed to answer three questions: whether per-chunk speedup translates into end-to-end speedup in static tasks, whether reduced action delay translates into better accuracy in dynamic tasks, and whether the shape of the task-level trend and the location of its sweet spot are hardware-dependent. The full experimental combinations, sweep ranges, and implementation details are reported in Appendix B and C.

4.1 Setup

Policy Models.

We evaluate policy models at different scales. We use MLP-Mixer [47, 46] and diffusion policy [11] models for simple control tasks, and we also use foundation-scale embodied models in complex environment tasks, including VLAs such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5] and DynamicVLA [52], and WAMs such as Cosmos-Policy [23] and LingBot-VA [25].

Optimization Methods.

For policy-intrinsic optimization, we use quantization, pruning, and sampling-step reduction to accelerate the model inference. To characterize task-level trends with fine granularity, we construct a series of progressively lightweight operating points for each method to adjust α\alpha. For execution-aware optimization, we follow the asynchronous inference settings in VLASH [46] and progressively vary the overlap depth n′n^{\prime}.

Compute Platforms.

We evaluate the latency of policy models’ inference on edge devices such as the Jetson AGX Orin [38] (denoted AGX 15W/30W/50W) and server-class GPUs, including the RTX 3090 [1] and the Ada 6000 [39]. The power of edge devices can be adjusted to achieve different levels of computational capability.

Simulation Task Setup.

We evaluate both task regimes defined in Section 3. For static tasks, we use LIBERO [32], RoboCasa [37], and RoboTwin-2.0 [10]. These benchmarks primarily involve manipulation tasks such as grasping and placing stationary objects, where the task-relevant object states remain effectively unchanged during policy inference. For dynamic tasks, we use Kinetix [36] and DOM [52]. These benchmarks’ task-relevant states continue to evolve during policy inference, and their latency-injection protocols allow us to emulate different inference delays.

Real-World Task Setup.

We further evaluate our observations on a real UR5e robotic arm [15]. In the static setting, the robot needs to pick up a cube on the tabletop and place it in a target box. In the dynamic setting, the robot needs to grasp a cube moving on a conveyor. These two settings share the same manipulation objective but differ in whether the task-relevant object state evolves during policy inference.

4.2 Empirical Finding 1: A Per-Step Speedup Need Not Speed Up the Static Task

As shown in Figure , across all four model–task pairs, lightweighting—policy-intrinsic (α\alpha) or execution-aware (n′n^{\prime})—monotonically reduces the per-chunk time TchunkT_{\rm chunk}, but action quality also declines, so the chunk count NN grows. Their product Ttask=N⋅TchunkT_{\rm task}=N\cdot T_{\rm chunk} thus depends on which trend dominates. In Figure (a), (c), and (d), NN stays nearly flat under mild lightweighting and inflates sharply past a task-specific operating point, so TtaskT_{\rm task} traces a U-shape with an interior minimum below the baseline. Figure (b) is the corner case: NN inflates from the very first optimization step, so no setting beats the baseline. Figure (e) and (f) visualize the underlying mechanism on a representative asynchronous trial: as n′n^{\prime} grows, the robot arm traces longer end-effector paths and makes more failed grasp attempts before completing the task.

4.3 Empirical Finding 2: An Imprecise but Faster Reaction Can Improve the Dynamic Task

On dynamic tasks, lightweighting—policy-intrinsic (α\alpha) or execution-aware (n′n^{\prime})—drives two competing trends: action quality qq falls because computation drops, but observation staleness z=Dact​ωenvz=D_{\rm act}\omega_{\rm env} also falls because the policy reacts on fresher observations. Task success rate PsuccP_{\rm succ} thus depends on which trend dominates. Figure 2(a) (Kinetix) shows the regime flip: under the zero-delay assumption (inf-hw), accuracy peaks usually at the larger sampling count ss; once realistic delay is injected to simulate AGX 15W’s inference latency, smaller ss becomes the better choice because the reaction-speed gain outweighs the per-step quality loss. Figure 2(b) (DOM-CR) sweeps both ss and the environment speed ωenv\omega_{\rm env}: at every speed, the best configuration is neither the lowest-delay nor the finest-action one, but an interior sweet spot that balances qq and zz; the sweet-spot location itself shifts with ωenv\omega_{\rm env}. Figure 2(c) visualizes the paradox in DOM-CR scene.

4.4 Empirical Finding 3: The Trend and Optimum Shifts with Hardware

Empirical Findings 1 and 2 established that a sweet spot may exist on both static and dynamic tasks. We next ask whether its location is hardware-dependent. To isolate the hardware effect, we fix the task and the lightweighting sweep, and vary only the inference hardware, which changes the inference-to-execution ratio ρ=Tinf/Tact\rho=T_{\rm inf}/T_{\rm act}. Figure 3(a) (static, async sweep over n′n^{\prime}): on high-performance hardware (ρ\rho small), the per-chunk speedup ηchunk\eta_{\rm chunk} is large enough that the gain from inference optimization outweighs the chunk-count inflation, so the sweet spot drifts toward more aggressive overlap; on low-performance hardware (ρ\rho large), the per-chunk gain shrinks while NN inflates rapidly, so the sweet spot retreats to milder overlap. Figure 3(b) (dynamic, sampling-step sweep over ss): on high-performance hardware, inference delay DactD_{\rm act} is no longer the dominant factor limiting accuracy, so the sweet spot favors larger ss where the policy retains higher action quality qq; on low-performance hardware, observation staleness zz dominates and the policy must trade off action quality against reaction speed, so the sweet spot shifts to smaller ss. Across both regimes, the sweet-spot location is qualitatively sensitive to the hardware compute budget; the quantitative derivation is in Appendix A.2.

4.5 Real-World Experiments

We conduct two real-world studies on a UR5e robot arm as shown in Figure 4. For the static task, we use a fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} model [5] and measure TinfT_{\rm inf} and TtaskT_{\rm task} over all successful trials under different sampling-step settings. Table 4.5 shows that the two metrics exhibit opposite trends as lightweighting becomes more aggressive. For the dynamic experiment, we use a fine-tuned diffusion policy model [11] and compute the score based on the relative position between the gripper and the cube. Table 4.5 shows that diffusion policies with fewer sampling steps can achieve higher dynamic-task scores, because their faster reaction outweighs the loss in action quality. Tables 4.5 and 4.5 further show that the sweet-spot step in both regimes shifts across hardware. Figures 4(c) and 4(d) visualize this static-task paradox at the trajectory level: as the sampling step decreases, the grasp-distance trace shows visibly more oscillation. Together, these two real-world studies provide physical evidence for the speedup paradox and corresponding hardware shift.

5 Conclusion

We present TISED, a task-level decomposition framework for analyzing lossy inference optimization in embodied policies. Beyond per-step latency, TISED decomposes optimization into per-chunk speedup, rollout chunk count, action delay, and compute-hardware dependence. Across policy-intrinsic and execution-aware optimization, which validated in both simulation and real-world UR5e experiments, we identify two paradoxes and one drift: (1) faster per-step inference can yield slower per-task time on static tasks; (2) less precise inference can yield higher success on dynamic tasks; and (3) the per-task sweet spot drifts with the deployment hardware. More fundamentally, these results elevate closed-loop computation to its own design axis, coupling speed, quality, dynamics, and hardware as joint determinants of task-level performance.

6 Limitations

This work has several limitations. (1) Our framework treats per-chunk time and chunk count as the dominant degrees of freedom; second-order effects such as scheduling jitter, and OS-level scheduling latency are abstracted away and may matter for more precise analysis. (2) For execution-aware optimization, we model asynchronous inference as a simplified overlap depth, not as a full server-client implementation; production schedulers may exhibit additional queueing or contention effects. (3) For the static tasks, we approximate NN as a function of action quality alone; other effects such as motion jerk and grasp stability is observed but not formally modeled. (4) For the dynamic tasks, extremely high-frequency interactions (e.g., table tennis) are out of scope. (5) Our real-world validation is restricted to a single UR5e platform and two task families; large-scale physical validation is left to future work.

Appendix A Detailed Analysis of the TISED (Section 3)

This section provides a quantitative interpretation of the task-level inference speedup effect decomposition (TISED) introduced in the main paper. Table 1 summarizes the notation used in the derivation.

Symbol Meaning Symbol Meaning
hh Compute hardware platform. ρh\rho_{h} Ratio Tinf,h/TactT_{\mathrm{inf},h}/T_{\mathrm{act}}.
α\alpha Policy-intrinsic inference-time ratio, with α∈[αmin,1]\alpha\in[\alpha_{\min},1]. n′n^{\prime} Discrete asynchronous overlap depth, with n′∈{0,…,n}n^{\prime}\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.
αmin\alpha_{\min} Smallest α\alpha whose policy accuracy remains above zero.
Tinf,hT_{\mathrm{inf},h} Baseline inference time on hh. TactT_{\mathrm{act}} Execution time of one atomic action.
nn Actions in one chunk. Tchunk,hbaseT_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{base}} Baseline action-chunk time.
Tchunk,hpl/eaT_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{pl/ea}} Optimized per-chunk time. Npl/eaN^{\mathrm{pl/ea}} Chunks required for task completion.
Ttask,hpl/eaT_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl/ea}} End-to-end completion time. Dact,hpl/eaD_{\mathrm{act},h}^{\mathrm{pl/ea}} Observation-to-action delay.
qq Action quality. ωenv\omega_{\mathrm{env}} Environment evolution rate.
zhz_{h} Staleness exposure Dact,h​ωenvD_{\mathrm{act},h}\omega_{\mathrm{env}}. Φ\Phi Task response function.
Psucc,hP_{\mathrm{succ},h} Modeled dynamic-task success rate.

A.1 When Does a “Sweet Spot” Exist?

A.1.1 Optimization Variables

Policy-Intrinsic Optimization.

We analyze the inference-time ratio α∈[αmin,1]\alpha\in[\alpha_{\min},1], where smaller α\alpha means more aggressive lightweighting. All derivatives with respect to α\alpha below are therefore taken in the direction of less aggressive lightweighting. When reading the same result along the optimization-strength direction used in the plots, the direction is reversed.

Execution-Aware Optimization.

We analyze the overlap depth n′∈{0,…,n}n^{\prime}\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, where larger n′n^{\prime} means more aggressive overlap between inference and action execution.

A.1.2 Static Tasks

Policy-Intrinsic Optimization.

For static tasks, we have

Ttask,hpl​(α)=Npl​(α)​Tchunk,hpl​(α),Tchunk,hpl​(α)=α​Tinf,h+n​Tact.T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)=N^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha),\qquad T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)=\alpha T_{\mathrm{inf},h}+nT_{\mathrm{act}}. (9)

Increasing α\alpha means moving toward a more conservative policy: action quality improves and the required chunk count decreases, i.e., d​Npl​(α)/d​α<0\mathrm{d}N^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)/\mathrm{d}\alpha<0, but each chunk becomes slower. These two monotone effects act in opposite directions on Ttask,hpl=Npl​Tchunk,hplT_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}=N^{\mathrm{pl}}T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}: mild lightweighting can be dominated by the per-chunk speedup, whereas aggressive lightweighting can be dominated by the growth of NplN^{\mathrm{pl}}. The derivative of Ttask,hplT_{\rm task,h}^{\rm pl} with respect to α\alpha can be written as a competition between the cost of slower chunks and the benefit of requiring fewer chunks:

d​Ttask,hpl​(α)d​α=Npl​(α)​Tinf,h⏟cost: slower chunks−[−d​Npl​(α)d​α]​(α​Tinf,h+n​Tact)⏟benefit: fewer chunks.\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}=\underbrace{N^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)T_{\mathrm{inf},h}}_{\text{cost: slower chunks}}-\underbrace{\left[-\frac{\mathrm{d}N^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\right]\left(\alpha T_{\mathrm{inf},h}+nT_{\mathrm{act}}\right)}_{\text{benefit: fewer chunks}}. (10)

An interior minimum occurs only when the derivative of the task time changes sign:

d​Ttask,hpl​(α)d​α|α=αmin<0,d​Ttask,hpl​(α)d​α|α=1>0.\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=\alpha_{\min}}<0,\qquad\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=1}>0. (11)

Otherwise, the shortest TtaskT_{\rm task} setting can lie at one endpoint.

Execution-Aware Optimization.

For execution-aware optimization, the corresponding objective is

Ttask,hea​(n′)=Nea​(n′)​Tchunk,hea​(n′),Tchunk,hea​(n′)=Tinf,h+n​Tact−min⁡{Tinf,h,n′​Tact}.T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=T_{\mathrm{inf},h}+nT_{\mathrm{act}}-\min\!\left\{T_{\mathrm{inf},h},n^{\prime}T_{\mathrm{act}}\right\}. (12)

Larger n′n^{\prime} means more aggressive overlap. Increasing n′n^{\prime} can reduce Tchunk,heaT_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{ea}} by hiding more inference behind action execution, but excessive overlap may increase NeaN^{\mathrm{ea}} because action quality or observation–execution alignment degrades. Let Δ​f​(n′)=f⁡(n′+1)−f⁡(n′)\Delta f(n^{\prime})=f(n^{\prime}+1)-f(n^{\prime}); then

Δ​Ttask,hea​(n′)\displaystyle\Delta T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}) =Ttask,hea​(n′+1)−Ttask,hea​(n′)\displaystyle=T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}+1)-T_{\mathrm{task},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}) (13)
=Δ​Nea​(n′)​Tchunk,hea​(n′+1)⏟cost: more chunks−Nea​(n′)​[−Δ​Tchunk,hea​(n′)]⏟benefit: faster chunks.\displaystyle=\underbrace{\Delta N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}+1)}_{\text{cost: more chunks}}-\underbrace{N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\left[-\Delta T_{\mathrm{chunk},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\right]}_{\text{benefit: faster chunks}}.

A.1.3 Dynamic Tasks

Policy-Intrinsic Optimization.

We model the policy-intrinsic dynamic-task success rate as

(15)

Here Φ\Phi is assumed to be monotone in the two arguments:

Φq=∂Φ∂q≥0,Φz=∂Φ∂z≤0,\Phi_{q}=\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial q}\geq 0,\qquad\Phi_{z}=\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\leq 0,

meaning that better action quality increases the modeled success rate, while larger staleness exposure decreases it. Increasing α\alpha usually improves action quality but also increases action delay: d​qpl​(α)/d​α≥0\mathrm{d}q^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)/\mathrm{d}\alpha\geq 0 and d​zhpl​(α)/d​α=Tinf,h​ωenv>0\mathrm{d}z_{h}^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha)/\mathrm{d}\alpha=T_{\mathrm{inf},h}\omega_{\mathrm{env}}>0. d​Psucc,hpld​α|α=αmin>0,d​Psucc,hpld​α|α=1<0.\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}P_{\mathrm{succ},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=\alpha_{\min}}>0,\qquad\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}P_{\mathrm{succ},h}^{\mathrm{pl}}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=1}<0. (17)

Otherwise, the best PsuccP_{\rm succ} setting can lie at one of the endpoints.

Execution-Aware Optimization.

The same response model becomes

Psucc,hea​(n′)≈Φ⁡(qea​(n′),zhea​(n′)),zhea​(n′)=max⁡{0,Tinf,h−n′​Tact}​ωenv.P_{\mathrm{succ},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\approx\Phi\!\left(q^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}),z_{h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\right),\qquad z_{h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})=\max\{0,T_{\mathrm{inf},h}-n^{\prime}T_{\mathrm{act}}\}\omega_{\mathrm{env}}. Increasing n′n^{\prime} means more aggressive execution-aware optimization. It can reduce staleness exposure by hiding inference behind action execution, but it may also degrade action quality or observation–execution alignment. Let Δ​f​(n′)=f⁡(n′+1)−f⁡(n′)\Delta f(n^{\prime})=f(n^{\prime}+1)-f(n^{\prime}). Then Δ​zhea​(n′)≤0\Delta z_{h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\leq 0 before overlap saturation, while Δ​qea​(n′)\Delta q^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}) can be negative when deeper overlap hurts action quality. A first-order finite-difference approximation gives

(19)

Δ​Psucc,hea​(0)>0,Δ​Psucc,hea​(n−1)<0.\Delta P_{\mathrm{succ},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(0)>0,\qquad\Delta P_{\mathrm{succ},h}^{\mathrm{ea}}(n-1)<0. (20)

Otherwise, the best PsuccP_{\rm succ} setting can lie at one endpoint.

A.2 How Does the “Sweet Spot” Move with Hardware?

A.2.1 Static Tasks: Take Execution-Aware Optimization as Example

We assume Nea​(n′+1)≥Nea​(n′)N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}+1)\geq N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}). The hardware-dependent sweet spot is

(n′)h⋆∈arg⁡minn′∈{0,…,n}​Nea​(n′)​(ρh+n−min⁡(ρh,n′)).(n^{\prime})_{h}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{n^{\prime}\in\{0,\ldots,n\}}N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime})\left(\rho_{h}+n-\min(\rho_{h},n^{\prime})\right). (21)

For the measured policy-intrinsic sweep,

A.3 Assumptions and Limitations

The analysis above is intentionally structured but lightweight. The analysis above makes several idealized assumptions. First, quantities such as Npl​(α)N^{\mathrm{pl}}(\alpha) and Nea​(n′)N^{\mathrm{ea}}(n^{\prime}) are specified only through their qualitative trends. Their concrete functional forms are task-dependent and must be obtained from empirical measurement. Second, Φ\Phi is used only as an abstract response function that describes how dynamic-task success depends on action quality and action delay. We do not assume that Φ\Phi has a fixed parametric form or represents a calibrated physical law.

Appendix B Simulation Experiment Details (Section 4.2, 4.3, 4.4)

This section describes how we design the optimization methods and choose the task regimes.

B.1 Optimization Method Settings

We summarize the policy models used in the main paper and their corresponding static and dynamic evaluation configurations in Tables 2 and 3.

Quantization.

At the operator level, we replace the FP16 linear layers in Transformer-based policies with integer linear operators, including int4-weight/int4-activation (W4A4) and int8-weight/int8-activation (W8A8) variants. The additional quantization and dequantization operators are fused into the surrounding operators to reduce inference overhead. We do not apply extra transformations such as smoothing [51] or rotation [3]. To obtain fine-grained operating points and expose potential sweet spots, we construct a progressive tier-10 quantization sweep as in [22]; the Cosmos-Policy quantization configurations are listed in Table 4.

Pruning.

For the pruning sweep, we use LingBot-VA [25] on RoboTwin tasks and implement a KV-cache pruning method. In the default RoboTwin setting, attn_window=72, which allocates up to 36 historical visual-latent chunks and 36 historical action chunks in the baseline cache. Our pruning further shortens the readable window inside this native cache. Let 𝒞<tvis\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{vis}}_{<t} and 𝒞<tact\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{act}}_{<t} denote the valid visual-latent and action KV slots retained by the native attention window before step tt. The pruned attention reads only

ℛt=RecentWlat⁡(𝒞<tvis)∪RecentWact⁡(𝒞<tact),ht=Attn⁡(qt,Kℛt,Vℛt),\mathcal{R}_{t}=\operatorname{Recent}_{W_{\mathrm{lat}}}\left(\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{vis}}_{<t}\right)\cup\operatorname{Recent}_{W_{\mathrm{act}}}\left(\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{act}}_{<t}\right),\qquad h_{t}=\operatorname{Attn}\!\left(q_{t},K_{\mathcal{R}_{t}},V_{\mathcal{R}_{t}}\right), (30)

where RecentW⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Recent}_{W}(\cdot) keeps the most recent WW slots of the corresponding cache stream. Figure 5 illustrates the difference between the native-window baseline and our read-window pruning. The pruned setting keeps cache writing unchanged but exposes only the most recent WlatW_{\mathrm{lat}} and WactW_{\mathrm{act}} entries to attention.

Table 5 lists the operating points used in the sweep. To make the pruning strength directly comparable across settings, we first report the total readable KV budget retained relative to the baseline. This normalized value decreases monotonically from base to p4, so smaller values indicate more aggressive lightweighting. The KV-budget columns then report the maximum number of readable historical tokens for the visual-latent and action streams. The chunk columns convert these token budgets using the RoboTwin configuration. Each visual-latent chunk contains 240 KV tokens, and each action chunk contains 32 KV tokens. For example, 1024/2561024/256 means that each action-generation step can read at most the most recent 1024 visual-latent KV entries and 256 action KV entries, corresponding to roughly 4.3 visual chunks and 8 action chunks.

Action-Generation Step-Count Reduction.

We reduce the number of action-generation steps used to generate each action chunk. We then evaluate a progressive step sweep to characterize the trade-off between computing speed and action quality.

Asynchronous Inference.

We adopt the simplified asynchronous-inference model from VLASH [46]. The overlap depth between inference and execution is controlled by n′n^{\prime}: at simulation step tt, the policy receives the stale observation from t−n′t-n^{\prime} steps earlier. This emulates delayed machine-vision input due to overlapping policy inference and action execution.

B.2 Task Settings

We group the simulation benchmarks according to the task regimes defined in the main paper: LIBERO, RoboCasa, and the LeRobot(RoboTwin) tasks are used as static-task benchmarks, while Kinetix and DOM-CR are used as dynamic-task benchmarks.

LIBERO.

LIBERO [32] is a tabletop manipulation benchmark suite designed to evaluate policy generalization and knowledge transfer across object, spatial, goal, and long-horizon task variations. We use it as a controlled static-task setting because the task-relevant object and goal states are assumed to remain unchanged during policy inference.

RoboCasa.

RoboCasa [37] provides large-scale simulated household manipulation tasks with diverse kitchen layouts, objects, and task instances. Despite the static-scene assumption, RoboCasa tasks are typically more challenging than those in LIBERO.

LeRobot.

LeRobot [9] is an open-source robot-learning ecosystem that standardizes datasets, policy training, and evaluation interfaces across simulated and real manipulation tasks. For LingBot-VA, the data and evaluation interface follow the LeRobot-style format, while the underlying simulated environments are generated from RoboTwin [10], a SAPIEN-based dual-arm manipulation benchmark with multi-camera observations and diverse bimanual tasks. These tasks are treated as static manipulation tasks because task-relevant objects do not deliberately move during policy inference.

Kinetix.

Kinetix [36] is a 2D physics-based control benchmark with procedurally designed tasks involving contact-rich interaction, object manipulation, locomotion, balance, and timing-sensitive control. The policy is an iterative, flow-style action generator with an MLP-Mixer architecture [46], and we vary the number of refinement steps in {1,3,5}\{1,3,5\} to trade off zero-delay action quality against inference latency. We evaluate both zero-delay inference, denoted as inf-hw in the main text, and hardware-induced delay. For the latter, we profile inference latency τ\tau and map it to an integer control-step delay d=round⁡(τ/33.33​ms)d=\mathrm{round}(\tau/33.33\mathrm{ms}), since Kinetix applies actions every two 16.67 ms physics steps. Consequently, different profiled latencies can fall into the same simulator delay bin.

DOM.

The Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark is introduced with DynamicVLA [52] to evaluate policies on moving-object manipulation, where the environment continues to evolve during inference delay. It organizes dynamic scenarios along three dimensions: interaction, perception, and generalization. We focus on Closed-loop Reactivity (CR), a sub-dimension of interaction that evaluates how quickly a policy adjusts to objects moving at different speeds. We vary the action expert’s refinement steps in {1,2,5,10}\{1,2,5,10\} and inject simulator delays calibrated to emulate inference latency on different hardware platforms. We evaluate object-motion speed scales of 100% and 125% relative to the original dataset. For each combination of object speed, refinement-step setting, and latency condition, we run 50 trials and report the task success rate and action delay.

B.3 Result Visualization

Figure 6 replots the four static-task tables in Section 4.2 as line charts. All three quantities are normalized by the corresponding baseline value in each panel. The star marks the operating point with the lowest TtaskT_{\mathrm{task}}.

Notably, the variation trends manifest differently across different tasks. For example, for the pick-and-place sink-to-counter task in Figure 6(a), NN remains roughly stable through moderate quantization, so the latency reduction dominates and the shortest per-task time appears at w4-t3. For the turn-off-microwave task in Figure 6(b), NN increases quickly even under mild quantization, so the full-precision baseline remains the shortest end-to-end time.

Appendix C Real-World Experiment Details (Section 4.5)

We use a UR5e robot arm [15] to validate the two task regimes in the physical world. The real-world robot setup follows UMI [12], with the mirrors on the gripper removed. The setup consists of a UR5e robot arm, a UMI gripper, and a GoPro camera for RGB observation. All experiments were conducted with the same robot arm speed setting of 30% and a control frequency of 10 Hz.

To evaluate how compute capability, i.e., ρ\rho, affects TtaskT_{\rm task} or task accuracy, we first profile the policy model’s inference latency TinfT_{\rm inf} across different hardware platforms. We then introduce a hardware-latency scaling factor λ\lambda on the RTX 4070 platform, i.e., Ttask,simulated=λ​Ttask,original,ρsimulated=λ​ρoriginalT_{\rm task,simulated}=\lambda T_{\rm task,original},\rho_{\rm simulated}=\lambda\rho_{\rm original}, which allows us to simulate the inference behavior of different compute platforms under the same task environment.

C.1 Static Experiment Settings

We collected 198 expert demonstrations using the UMI gripper and fine-tuned the π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5] model for 30,000 training steps using LoRA [19]. During LoRA fine-tuning, we initialized the policy from the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-base model, which consists of two components: a VLM backbone and an action expert. The VLM backbone is PaliGemma [4], composed of a SigLIP vision encoder and a Gemma-2B language model, while the action expert is a 300M Gemma model. We fine-tuned both components with a learning rate of 2.5×10−52.5\times 10^{-5} and a batch size of 32.

The static manipulation task requires the robot to pick up a red cube on the tabletop and place it into a target box. A trial is considered successful only if the gripper fingers open and release the cube into the target box. Each rollout started from the same predefined initial position. For each rollout setting, we conducted 5 trials and reported the corresponding task performance.

C.2 Dynamic Experiment Settings

We collected 196 expert demonstrations using the UMI gripper and trained the diffusion policy [11] for 130 epochs. The diffusion policy model is composed of a pretrained ViT vision encoder and a DiT action decoder. The DiT module was trained from scratch with a learning rate of 3.0×10−43.0\times 10^{-4}. For the visual encoder, we initialized the ViT backbone from the CLIP [42] pretrained ViT-L/14 model [14] and trained it with a learning rate of 3.0×10−53.0\times 10^{-5} and a batch size of 32.

The dynamic manipulation task requires the robot to grasp the red cube as it moves on a conveyor. We evaluate grasping performance using a three-level score: 2 indicates that the red cube is successfully grasped and held by both gripper fingers; 1 indicates that only one gripper finger contacts the red cube; and 0 indicates that neither gripper finger reaches the red cube. This scoring criterion reports both the robot’s reaction speed and motion quality in the dynamic task. The conveyor moved at a constant speed of 6.25 cm/s during evaluation. For each rollout setting, we conducted 30 trials. Specifically, we used three fixed initial positions and performed 10 trials for each position.

Appendix D Additional Discussions

D.1 About “Successful-Only Trial’s Chunks”

Following the successful-episode reporting protocol in prior work [29], we report chunk number and completion time only over successful rollouts:

Nsucc=𝔼⁡[N∣success],Ttask,succ=𝔼⁡[Ttask∣success].N_{\mathrm{succ}}=\mathbb{E}[N\mid\mathrm{success}],\qquad T_{\mathrm{task,succ}}=\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathrm{task}}\mid\mathrm{success}]. (31)

The successful-only convention avoids an artifact of simulator rollouts: when a task fails, the simulator may continue executing additional chunks and corrective attempts until the rollout horizon is reached. Including timeout trajectories would inflate NN and TtaskT_{\rm task}, so the averages would reflect the simulator termination rule instead of the efficiency of completed executions.

D.2 Stability and Motion Smoothness

Prior work [29] analyzed in simulation several embodied-efficiency indicators that deteriorate as the degree of lightweighting increases, such as jerk. We additionally conduct real-world experiments on the UR5e platform.

For an end-effector trajectory 𝐱0,…,𝐱K−1\mathbf{x}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{K-1} sampled at interval Δ​t\Delta t, we quantify motion jerk as

J^=1K−3​∑k=0K−4‖𝐱k+3−3​𝐱k+2+3​𝐱k+1−𝐱kΔ​t3‖22.\widehat{J}=\frac{1}{K-3}\sum_{k=0}^{K-4}\left\|\frac{\mathbf{x}_{k+3}-3\mathbf{x}_{k+2}+3\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}_{k}}{\Delta t^{3}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (32)

We report J^\widehat{J} over static task trials for each step setting in Table 7. The result shows that stronger lightweighting leads to larger motion jerk in real-world execution. This result is consistent with the simulator observation in work [29], indicating that aggressive lightweighting can reduce the policy model’s computation while degrading physical motion quality.
